issues.item: Triggers: Power Imbalance: Being in a situation where someone has power over me
issues.explanation: The trigger 'being in a situation where someone has power over me' is hard to reconcile with the stated trauma type of natural disaster and with the rest of the profile, which otherwise emphasizes alarm/reactivity and fragmented recall rather than interpersonal domination or coercion. For this trauma type, this item introduces an implausible trigger theme not supported elsewhere in threat, memory, or appraisals.

issues.item: Maladaptive Strategies: Avoid Medical Cues: Hospitals/ Ambulances/ Physical Examinations
issues.explanation: Avoiding hospitals/ambulances/physical examinations is not well supported by the rest of the profile for a natural-disaster trauma. There are no memory or threat items involving injury treatment, medical rescue, or bodily harm, so this strategy appears to target a symptom theme not represented elsewhere. In contrast, the profile is centered on generalized alarm, shouting, unpredictability, and fragmented memory.

issues.item: Self-Harm: hurt myself physically to release overwhelming feelings
issues.explanation: Self-harm is hard to reconcile with the rest of the profile and trauma context: the other selected items describe a classic hyperarousal/re-experiencing natural-disaster PTSD presentation with avoidance and overeating, but no accompanying items suggest the kind of shame, self-punitive appraisal, dissociative affect regulation, or broader emotion-dysregulation pattern that would make physical self-harm clinically coherent here. It stands out as addressing a symptom process not otherwise represented in the five components.

Alcohol smell is not impossible, but in this profile it is weakly anchored to the reported trauma type and the rest of the item set. The other triggers (unpredictability, shouting) fit a danger/hyperarousal formulation, whereas alcohol smell implies a very specific sensory trauma cue that is not supported by the memory or threat items. Given a natural-disaster index trauma, this trigger is difficult to explain clinically without additional corroborating content.

vignette: Kwame was fifty-two when the hurricane tore through the coastal district. He stood on the metal grating of the municipal archive roof, wrestling with heavy tarp straps, when the wind shifted without warning. One moment the storm was a steady, heavy roar; the next, a steel support beam gave way with a sharp, explosive crack that echoed like a detonation. People on the ground began shouting, their voices rising in overlapping panic, and the sudden gusts whipped debris against the scaffolding. The storm passed over the course of hours, but it was the unpredictability of those shifting winds, the sharp cracks, and the rising shouts that settled into his routine. In the weeks that followed, Kwame found his body bracing before his mind caught up. A backfiring car would make his shoulders hike to his ears; a dropped metal tray in the breakroom sent a jolt through his ribs. He would catch himself breathing hard, certain the storm was returning, even though the sky was clear. His wife, Nia, noticed how he started leaving the house earlier to avoid rush hour, skipping gatherings where conversations grew too loud or plans shifted too quickly. He kept his mind occupied-tuning radios, solving crosswords in the paper, watching construction videos on his tablet-and sitting still made the quiet feel heavy. When he finally let himself remember the night on the roof, the fragments would not hold together. He found himself pushing the memory away before he could fully recall it, letting the details slip back into the quiet. The picture remained incomplete, parts of the night drifting just out of reach. On more than one occasion, the weight of the tarp straps would return in a wave, and for a few seconds he was standing on the roof again, the wind biting his neck. When the pieces did surface, a hot surge of rage would rise in his chest, fierce and sudden. His work at the county bomb disposal unit became a familiar ground, yet also a place where his reactions played out in plain sight. During a live training exercise, a sudden hydraulic hiss from a cutting torch made him step back, his body already coiled, before the technician even called out. The unpredictability of the unit's dispatch schedule mirrored the way the storm had arrived. He learned to navigate the workshop with a quiet rhythm, deliberately taking the stairs instead of the elevator to avoid the sudden jolt of the doors, carrying snacks he ate methodically to manage the rising tension. When his supervisor scheduled an unexpected site visit, Kwame felt the familiar tightness in his throat and quietly declined, preferring the controlled clutter of his workbench to the shifting demands of the office. His recent intake screening yielded a PCL-5 score of sixty-four, a number that felt accurate to the weight he had been carrying. Now at fifty-five, Kwame sits across from me with his hands folded, the calluses from wire cutters still visible. He came in because the quiet at home no longer feels safe. He worries that if he stops moving or stops eating, the tension will build until he snaps. What he hopes for is not the complete erasure of the memories, but the space to remember them without the room tilting beneath him. He is learning that the body's early warning is not a signal of catastrophe, and that the shouting of a crowd or the crack of a door is not a return of the storm, but simply the world moving forward.
